   Intel shares drop 21% on Israel factory blast, PC weakness

 The October explosion at Intel’s Kiryat Gat factory in Israel killed two and seriously injured one.
 PHOTO: REUTERS
 Published   Oct 30, 2026, 08:15 AM
 Updated   Oct 30, 2026, 08:15 AM
 Set as preferred source Summarise Intel shares fell 21% after a deadly blast at its Israel factory and weak PC demand. The company warned of about US$600 million lost revenue over two quarters.
 CEO Lip-Bu Tan said Intel faces “manufacturing supply shortages” and “the unprecedented memory crunch”. Finance chief David Zinsner said the Kiryat Gat fab should restart production by Nov 1 after a two-week shutdown.
 Intel cut its fourth-quarter outlook to US$15 billion-US$16 billion in revenue and 25 US cents a share profit. It also expects PC weakness to last into the first half of 2027.
 AI generated
 SANTA CLARA, California – Intel shares plunged 21% on Oct 29 after the chipmaker said a deadly explosion at its Israel factory would erase roughly US$600 million (S$770 million) in revenue over two quarters, while a faltering PC market could dent sales through the first half of 2027.
 A below-estimates forecast came as exponential increases in memory prices have weighed on sales.
 Unless the stock recovers from the after-hours loss during the session on Oct 30, Intel would shed over US$80 billion in market value.
 The gloomy outlook reverberated across the chip sector.
 Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, Micron, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings’ US-listed shares fell between 1% and 6% in extended trading.
 “I’m disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter,” Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said on a conference call with analysts. “We face near-term challenges, including manufacturing supply shortages, the unprecedented memory crunch, and the resulting softness in PC demand.”
 The October explosion at its Kiryat Gat, Israel factory, or fab, killed two and seriously injured one, according to local media reports.
 Finance chief David Zinsner said Intel planned to start ramping up production at the facility by Nov 1 after a two-week shutdown.
 The fourth-quarter revenue outlook has been reduced by roughly US$300 million and its gross margin outlook by about 200 basis points, Zinsner said in an interview with Reuters. He said the company expects a similar revenue impact in the first quarter.
 Intel is in the process of determining which wafers are salvageable for use and sale after the blast.
 “We’re still assessing all of the wafers to see which ones are usable and which ones aren’t, so we’ll have to see whether there is an impact that stretches beyond that,” Zinsner said.
 The Kiryat Gat fab largely produces data centre chips using the company’s 10 nanometre manufacturing process.
 “The explosion at Kiryat Gat, one of Intel’s major manufacturing sites, is unfortunate and brought down Intel’s capacity,” said Hendi Susanto, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds. “The question is whether Intel can build capacity fast enough to capture it.”
 Slowing PC sales
 Before the after-hours drop on Oct 29, Intel’s stock had more than doubled in 2026.
 Now, investors must weigh ongoing manufacturing constraints and soft PC demand against strong demand for its AI server chips and efforts to revive growth through a costly foundry expansion.
 Zinsner said he expects the PC slowdown will continue through the first half of 2027.
 The company expects PC revenue to decline in the mid-20% range for its fourth quarter, Zinsner said in the interview.
 Sales in Intel’s PC chip business fell 5% to US$8.10 billion, missing estimates of US$8.98 billion.
 Investors have been watching for signs that demand has stabilised despite the company’s expectation for a soft personal-computing market in the second half of 2026 and into 2027.

 “Client computing is still a big factor in Intel’s earnings so while it is likely short-term, it will still impact earnings for the near term and I think that’s the biggest issue,” said Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy.
 The results also put a spotlight on Intel’s funding plans.
 In August, the company raised US$23 billion from an upsized share offering, as it seeks to challenge industry leaders such as TSMC in contract chip manufacturing.
 Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue between US$15 billion and US$16 billion, below analysts’ average estimate of US$17.07 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
 Adjusted profit is expected to be 25 US cents per share, trailing estimates of 43 US cents.
 Turnaround plans
 On the conference call with investors, Zinsner said Intel does not expect to have positive cash flow in 2026 as it invests in expanding manufacturing capacity.
 In July, the company raised its 2026 capital spending forecast to US$20 billion from US$18 billion and said 2027 spending would increase significantly to expand manufacturing capacity.
 Tan has been leading the company’s turnaround after it fell behind Nvidia, whose graphics processors dominate the AI boom.
 Intel’s contract manufacturing, or foundry business, is a key part of his revival strategy.
 In the third quarter ended Sept 26, revenue rose 21% to US$16.51 billion, largely in line with estimates of US$16.50 billion. Adjusted profit came in at 52 US cents per share, beating estimates of 40 US cents. REUTERS
